report:
Based on the evidence, your assessment appears correct.

**Report**

The largest and most rigorous trial—the Phase III, multicenter, placebo-controlled study by Beal and colleagues (JAMA Neurology, 2014, N=600)—found that high-dosage CoQ10 (1,200 mg or 2,400 mg/day) provided no benefit over placebo in slowing functional decline in early Parkinson's disease and was terminated early for futility (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/1851409). This confirmed and extended earlier findings from a smaller NINDS NET-PD futility trial, which found the drug did not meet pre-specified thresholds warranting further phase III testing based on motor progression measures (https://www.neurology.org/doi/10.1212/01.wnl.0000250355.28474.8e).

An earlier Phase II dose-ranging trial (Shults et al., JAMA Neurology) had suggested a possible modest slowing of functional decline with the highest dose tested, but this was a small, hypothesis-generating study, not confirmed in the larger, definitive trial (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/782965).

A subsequent meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (Zhu et al., 2016, published in *Neurological Sciences*) similarly concluded that CoQ10 showed no significant improvement on UPDRS motor scores or overall disease progression compared to placebo, while confirming it is generally safe and well-tolerated (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10072-016-2757-9).

**Conclusion:** The weight of evidence—an initial promising small trial followed by a large, definitive Phase III RCT and meta-analyses—supports that CoQ10 does not meaningfully improve movement/motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease. It remains under some investigation for non-motor symptoms, but for motor outcomes specifically, current high-quality evidence does not support its use.
